{"gloss_range":"complete non-clausal three-letter opener: rootless, uninflected, visually compact, recited as separated letter-names, semantically opaque, and meaningful through opening position, recurrence, sound, and the immediate move toward the following question rather than ordinary lexical predication","prose":"{{ar:الٓمٓ}} ({{tr:alif lām mīm}}) is a complete ayah made of disconnected letter-names, not a noun, verb, declined phrase, governed particle construction, or hidden clause. Its grammar is exclusion from ordinary syntax: no lexical root, case, subject, predicate, object, attachment target, valency, or scope relation is available inside 29:1. That inertness does not make the opener empty; it makes sign-status and recited sound the first event of the surah before any proposition appears. The opacity resets attention, so the listener has to receive the opening signal itself before the next ayah asks {{ar:أَحَسِبَ}} ({{tr:a-ḥasiba}}) (29:2). Several functions can coexist around the same signs: solemn or oath-like register, attention call, discourse-unit marker, metalinguistic display, and inimitability pressure through ordinary letters, while the local grammar selects none of them as a governed lexical statement. The ayah therefore presents the material units of speech before referential wording: {{ar:ا}} ({{tr:alif}}), {{ar:ل}} ({{tr:lām}}), and {{ar:م}} ({{tr:mīm}}) are heard as letter-names rather than parsed as a root-derived word. The written surface is one compact token, yet recitation unfolds it into three separately salient names marked by madd and possible waqf separation; root-family and stem analysis stop at that boundary. A classical initial-expansion reading can remain latent because the letters can stand as signs, but the text does not turn them into expanded lexical words. Across the corpus, this exact opener recurs at 2:1, 3:1, 29:1, 30:1, 31:1, and 32:1, with 29:1-32:1 forming a contiguous ALM block, so this opening belongs to a constrained Quranic threshold pattern rather than an isolated cryptic item. The ayah is also liminal at its right edge: the standard reading lets {{ar:الٓمٓ}} ({{tr:alif lām mīm}}) close as a sealed utterance, while the connected reading {{ar:المَ احَسِبَ}} ({{tr:alif lām mīma-ḥasiba}}) carries the final {{ar:م}} ({{tr:mīm}}) into the following question (29:2). That variant does not replace the standard pause, but it makes the boundary itself audible as a place where the opener can both stop and lean forward. Sonically, the sequence moves from open glottal onset through tongue-lateral shaping to bilabial nasal closure; because lexical meaning is withheld, that physical path of speech becomes part of the reader-facing surface. The main payoff is convergence: no clause, no root, semantic withholding, alphabetic self-reference, compact writing, separated recitation, ALM recurrence, bodily sound movement, and the pause-or-connection boundary all make the surah begin as a threshold before the interrogative discourse of 29:2.","root_display":"no lexical root","root_gloss_range":null,"surface_display":"{{ar:الٓمٓ}} ({{tr:alif lām mīm}})"}
